paras: The killing of Oliver Lott took place at Tunnel Springs, Alabama, on August 22, 1905, when a posse of white citizens shot Lott, a Black mill laborer, to death in a house where he had barricaded himself. Lott was accused of shooting two white carpenters, John and Harry Helton, in a quarrel over a debt, and of fatally wounding the posse's leader, the mill owner G. Talley. The Associated Press spread the story nationally as a 'negro murderer' killed by a posse; an Alabama report added that the posse's fire also wounded the house's Black owner.

Tunnel Springs was a station on the Louisville and Nashville railroad about sixty miles south of Selma, near Beatrice, where Talley ran a saw mill. The Heltons worked there as carpenters, and Lott had also worked at the mill until a few days earlier. The Montgomery Advertiser's Selma bureau wrote that he had 'overdrew his salary' and stopped coming to work, while the Birmingham Age-Herald said he had quit owing his employer money.

According to the Age-Herald's Selma correspondent, the Heltons went to Lott's house on the morning of August 22, told him to come to work and asked him to pay what he owed. In that account Lott seized a Winchester and fired twice, killing John Helton and wounding Harry; the Advertiser instead described a fight in which Lott drew a pistol. Lott then went to the house of another Black man nearby and barricaded himself inside, and the owner 'was compelled to stay in the house with him.'

Talley gathered 'a number of citizens' and went to Lott's hiding place to arrest him for the murder of John Helton. When Lott refused to surrender, a shot from the house struck Talley in the neck; the Age-Herald said he was standing at his horse's head after driving up with a Mr. Farrior. The posse then fired into the house, 'a hundred shots' by the Age-Herald's count, after the citizens 'determined to capture the negro dead or alive.' The walls were flimsy, and when no more shots came from inside the posse broke in the door and found Lott dead on the floor, his body riddled with bullets. One of the shots struck the owner of the house, who was not named; he escaped further injury and went to a doctor.

No train could bring a Selma physician that night; Dr. J. P. Furniss arrived on the morning of August 23, shortly before Talley died at about ten o'clock. Harry Helton's wound was described as serious and possibly fatal. The Advertiser reported 'considerable fear' for Black residents of the neighborhood but said all had quieted down. No report of an inquest into Lott's death, or of any arrest, appears in the coverage.

White Alabama papers wrote in the posse's terms: the Montgomery Advertiser headlined 'Two White Men Killed' and 'Deadly Work of Bad Negro's Revolver', and the Age-Herald's 'Citizens Capture Slayer' treated Lott's death as a capture, adding that he 'was finally captured, that is his body was found full of holes.' The Associated Press version appeared in the San Antonio Daily Light, the New-York Tribune and the Alexandria Gazette under headlines such as 'Negro Murderer Killed by Posse' and 'Negro Kills Two Men.'

A shorter Selma wire, printed in the Topeka State Journal, the Los Angeles Herald and the Salt Lake Herald, said the posse set the house afire, and Topeka headlined 'Posse Burns House Over His Head.' The Raleigh News and Observer ran the AP text a day later as 'A Desperate Negro Killed', with the posse described as 'A score of citizens.' Later briefs called Lott 'a negro desperado', while a Texas paper used the word 'mob', writing that 'A mob slew the negro.' No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press, so every surviving account came from white correspondents and wire editors.

The short wire versions say the house was burned with Lott's body in the ruins, but the fuller Alabama accounts describe only gunfire and a broken-in door. The papers also differ on the debt, which the AP placed with the Heltons and the Alabama and Florida reports placed with Talley's mill.

reader.title: Killing of Oliver Lott
bases: A citizens' posse led by a mill owner surrounded the house where Oliver Lott, accused of killing John Helton, had barricaded himself, and shot him to death after he fired on them (A2, A3, A4).

A group of citizens ('a score' in A21, 'a hundred shots' in A3) killed Lott while trying to arrest him for a killing, but he was armed, at large and firing on them, no officer or deputization is mentioned either way, and the papers describe an armed standoff rather than a seizure; only two brief reprints call the posse 'a mob' (A20) (A2, A3, A4).

Two separate Selma correspondents (A3, A4) and the AP/Birmingham News report (A2) agree that Lott shot the Heltons, fatally wounded Talley from a barricaded house and was killed by the posse's gunfire.

accounts.label: AP / Birmingham News special
accounts.gist: Lott shot the Heltons in a quarrel over a debt owed them, refused to surrender to Talley's posse and fired on it; the posse fired on the house and found his body riddled.

accounts.label: Short Selma wire
accounts.gist: Same sequence, but the posse fired into the building 'and set it afire', and the body was found in the ruins.

accounts.label: Birmingham Age-Herald Selma correspondent
accounts.gist: Lett had quit owing Talley money; when the Heltons came to his house he fired a Winchester, then holed up in another Black man's house; Talley was shot while holding his horse, and the citizens fired a hundred shots into the house, wounding the homeowner and killing Lett.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser bureau
accounts.gist: Lett had overdrawn his pay; a quarrel with the Heltons turned into a fight and he drew a pistol; the posse shot through the flimsy walls after Talley was hit and broke in to find him dead on the floor.

accounts.label: Gainesville Sun Selma dispatch
accounts.gist: Lott owed Talley a bill handed to the Heltons to collect; he was pursued by armed men, cornered and 'shot to pieces'.

framing.detail: Alabama papers called Lott a 'Bad Negro' and the 'slayer', headlined 'Two White Men Killed' and 'Citizens Capture Slayer', and treated the killing as a capture.
National papers ran the AP item under headlines such as 'Negro Kills Two Men' and 'Negro Murderer Killed by Posse'.
Short versions headlined the posse's act ('Posse Burns House Over His Head', 'Posse Killed Him'), and one brief wrote 'A mob slew the negro'.

info: The Heltons were shot and the posse besieged the house on Aug. 22, 1905 ('yesterday morning' in a Selma dispatch of Aug. 23); Talley died about 10 a.m. on Aug. 23. Wire copy is datelined Aug. 23.
Tunnel (Tunnell) Springs, Ala., at or near G. Talley's saw mill, about two miles from Beatrice, some 60 miles south of Selma on the Pensacola division of the Louisville & Nashville railroad.
Oliver Lott (also printed Lett), a Black laborer, killed by the posse; an unnamed Black man whose house Lott occupied, wounded by the posse's fire.
Accused of shooting and killing John Helton and wounding Harry Helton, white carpenters at Talley's mill, in a quarrel over a debt, and then of fatally shooting G. Talley from the barricaded house.
A posse of local citizens led by G. Talley, owner of the saw mill; a Mr. Farrior drove with Talley.
